newsitem.title: GERMANY: Algeria FIS leader's sons convicted in Germany.
newsitem.headline: Algeria FIS leader's sons convicted in Germany.

text.p: A German court on Monday convicted two sons of detained Algerian fundamentalist opposition leader Abassi Madani of belonging to an outlawed support group for anti-government forces in Algeria.

Salim Abassi, 30, and his brother Ikbal, 26, who fled to Germany in 1992 and were allowed to stay as political refugees, were found guilty of belonging to a criminal organisation and forging official documents for fellow Algerian fundamentalists.

Salim, who was also convicted of explosives offences, was sentenced to two years and eight months and Ikbal to two years and four months in jail. But the court failed to establish whether their group had also been trading arms illegally to support of an Islamic armed struggle in Algeria.

"The aim of their criminal grouping was to provide persecuted Islamists with false passports and other forged documents," presiding judge Jutta Magiera-Steinacker told the court in Duesseldorf in the judgement.
"The fact that their aims had a humanitarian aspect in their desire to help fellow countrymen who were being persecuted acted as mitigating circumstances," she said.
The court said it could not establish whether two other Algerians, Nasr-Eddine Layachi Hemaz, 31, and Mahmoud Logbi, 26, had also been members of the Abassis' group
But it sentenced Hemaz to 31 months in jail for illegal arms trade and Logbi to 10 months for document forgery.
The judge said it helped that all four admitted the charges but, as Moslems, said they acted out of religious conviction.

The men had spent about two years in custody after German authorities cracked down on Algerian fundamentalists using the country as a base to support an armed conflict against Algeria's military rulers.
A court spokesman said they were unlikely to go to jail now because they had already spent so much time in remand.

Prosecutors initially accused the men of being members of a gun-running group that worked independently but kept conspiratorial links with other Islamic fundamentalists in France, Italy, Belgium and Algeria.

Salim's conviction for violating the law on explosives related to a detonator found in the chimney of the family home in western Germany. The judges dismissed his claim he was keeping the item for a friend and did not know what it was.
"He is too intelligent not to have realised what this detonator was for," Magiera-Steinacker told the court.

Although prosecutors argued the men were all members of a gun-running ring, only Hemaz was actually convicted of weapons smuggling charges. The judge said he had hired a German to drive to Hungary to buy old Soviet-made weapons there.

"He drove to Hungary in the summer of 1994 and bought at least 35 fully automatic Kalashnikov guns," the judge said, adding Hemaz then had the guns recomissioned in Germany but had not got as far as selling them.

Prosecutors said the group had shipped around 100 assault rifles, over 30 machine pistols, 20 repeating rifles, 15 hand guns, eight pump guns and assorted ammunition and explosives to Morocco and Algeria between March 1993 and April 1994.
The weapons were allegedly sent to the Armed Islamic Group (GIA) and the Islamic Salvation Army (AIS), on the military wing of the fundamentalist Islamic Salvation Front (FIS).

But prosecutors dropped gun-running charges against the others saying the case would take far too long if they pursued the investigation to the end. Prosecutor Volker Brinkmann told journalists after the trial he was satisfied with the verdict.
"We requested help from seven states including Algerian and Morocco, but their help was not always forthcoming and we didn't get all the documents we wanted," Brinkmann said.
The Abassis' father, Abassi Madani, is co-founder of the FIS, which took up arms against Algeria's military rulers after they intervened in 1992 to scrap a general election the FIS was set to win.
Abassi Madani was sentenced to 12 years' jail in 1991 in Algeria. He was put under house arrest in 1994.
